**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Computer Science 2 (0795), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Answer any SIX questions. All questions carry 17 marks each. For your guidance, the appropriate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.

questions.enonce_markdown: State what you understand by the term System Development Life Cycle. (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**System Development Life Cycle (1 mark)**

The System Development Life Cycle (SDLC) is the structured series of phases followed to plan, create, test, put into use and maintain an information system: for example preliminary investigation and feasibility study, systems analysis, system design, implementation (coding), testing, installation (changeover) and maintenance. The phases are carried out in order, and each phase produces documents (deliverables) used by the next.

questions.enonce_markdown: A school has expanded rapidly. A system analyst is employed to plan the introduction of a computer system which will store student records and details of student marks. For two distinct areas describe what the system analysts should report on during feasibility study. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Feasibility study (4 marks)**

The feasibility study decides whether the proposed system is worth developing. The analyst reports on, for example (any two areas, 2 marks each):

- **Technical feasibility.** Whether the hardware, software and technical skills available can support the system: how many computers, the server, the database software, the network between the offices, the storage needed for the records and marks of all students, backup and security; whether the existing equipment can be used or new equipment must be bought, and whether the staff can operate the system or need training.
- **Economic feasibility.** A cost-benefit analysis: the costs (equipment, software, development, installation, training, running and maintenance costs) are compared with the benefits (less paper and time spent on records and on computing averages, fewer errors, faster production of report cards), to show whether the system pays for itself and in how long.
- **Operational feasibility (alternatives: legal, schedule).** Whether the system will fit the way the school works and be accepted by the teachers and the administration, and whether the staff will be willing and able to use it; (legal) whether the keeping of students' personal data respects the data protection rules; (schedule) whether the system can be ready before the beginning of the school year.

questions.enonce_markdown: After determining the information requirements of users of an organization, briefly discuss four main phases or activities involved in information systems development, from analyzing systems need to testing and maintaining the system, for each phase or activity, your answer should describe its activities, the deliverables expected, and EITHER benefits OR challenges expected. (12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Four phases of information systems development (12 marks, 3 marks per phase)**

Applied to the school system, the four phases below follow the requirements already determined. (Any four phases between analysis and maintenance, for example implementation and testing taken as two separate phases, are accepted.)

| Phase | Activities | Deliverables | Benefit or challenge |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Systems analysis (analysing the system needs)** | Study the current system by interviews, questionnaires, observation and examination of documents (registers, mark sheets); find the problems; list the requirements of the users; model the data and processes (data flow diagrams). | Requirements specification, data flow diagrams, problem statement, system proposal. | *Benefit:* a clear and agreed idea of what the system must do, so that costly mistakes are avoided later. *(Challenge: users who cannot state their needs, or who disagree.)* |
| **2. System design** | Design the database (entity relationship diagram, tables and keys), the input screens and reports (report card layout), the processes (flowcharts or pseudocode), the security and the hardware and software to use. | Design specification: ER diagram, table structures, screen and report layouts, program specifications, test plan. | *Benefit:* a blueprint from which the programmers can work, and errors are much cheaper to correct on paper than in the finished system. *(Challenge: a design that is too rigid for changing needs.)* |
| **3. Implementation and testing** | Code the programs (or configure the package), create the database, convert and enter the existing records, install the equipment, train the users; test each module (unit test), the modules together (integration test), the whole system (system test) and acceptance test with the users, using normal, extreme and wrong test data. | Working system, tested programs, converted data, test plan and test reports, user manual and trained users, acceptance sign-off. | *Benefit:* errors are found and corrected before live use, and the users are sure the system does what was specified. *(Challenges: data conversion errors, resistance to change, time taken by the tests.)* |
| **4. Maintenance (and evaluation)** | After installation, correct errors found in use (corrective), adapt the system to new needs such as a new class or new grading rules (adaptive), improve its performance (perfective), keep backups. | Updated programs and documentation, maintenance log, new versions. | *Challenge:* maintenance is long and costly (often the largest part of the cost of the system) and requires good documentation; *benefit:* the system stays useful and reliable. |
